23c00d1c-4563-4335-983f-737a8bf981ae.title: What is Unseen Poetry?
23c00d1c-4563-4335-983f-737a8bf981ae.content_html:
The Unseen Poem Is Always Paired

In some courses the unseen poem is a task on its own. In this course it is not. The unseen poem is printed beside a named poem from the anthology cluster you have studied, and the two are joined by a shared theme. Your job is to read the new poem quickly, then set it against a poem you already know well.

Your class studies one anthology cluster from a choice of three: Love and Relationships, Conflict, or Youth and Age. Each cluster holds fifteen poems written since 1789, mixing literary heritage poets such as Emily Brontë and Lord Byron with modern voices. Whichever cluster you study, the unseen poem you meet in the exam will be chosen to link to it thematically.

Key Fact

The poetry section is worth 40 marks and splits into two parts of 20 marks each. Part (a) compares a named anthology poem with a thematically linked unseen poem — both are printed for you. Part (b) asks you to explore one other poem from your cluster, chosen by you and written about from memory. Part (b) involves no comparison at all.

What the Question Actually Looks Like

Part (a) begins by naming both poems and telling you which is which. It then gives you a single comparative instruction — something like “Compare how these poems present the wish for an end to conflict” — followed by three bullet prompts:

  • ideas and attitudes in each poem
  • tone and atmosphere in each poem
  • the effects of the language and structure used

The bullets are there to shape your answer, and they tell you that method matters as much as meaning. Part (b) is worded more broadly: “Explore in detail one other poem from your anthology which presents…” and repeats the theme in a slightly broader form.

Love and Relationships ranges from John Keats’s sonnet ‘Bright Star’ and Emily Brontë’s ‘Love and Friendship’ to modern poems such as Rita Dove’s ‘Flirtation’ and James Fenton’s ‘In Paris with You’.

Conflict stretches from Mary Lamb’s ‘Envy’ and Lord Byron’s ‘The Destruction of Sennacherib’ to Denise Levertov, John Agard and Imtiaz Dharker. Note that the cluster is called Conflict, not War — a quarrel, an injustice or a divided mind all count.

Youth and Age includes William Blake’s ‘Holy Thursday’ and Derek Walcott’s ‘Love After Love’. Whatever your cluster, learn its fifteen poems by theme as well as by title — part (b) is chosen by you, so pick the poem you can write about most confidently.

Which Skills Earn the Marks

Only two assessment objectives are credited in the poetry section. AO1 rewards a critical, informed personal response supported by textual references. AO2 rewards analysis of the language, form and structure a poet uses to create meanings and effects, with accurate terminology. In part (a), AO2 is the dominant objective. In part (b) the two carry equal weight.

Key Fact

Context is not assessed in the poetry section — you cannot know who wrote the unseen poem, so historical background earns nothing here. Neither is spelling, punctuation and grammar: that is credited in the Shakespeare section instead. Every mark in the poetry section comes from your reading of the poems and your analysis of how they work.

What Examiners Reward

Reports on this paper are consistent about what separates strong answers. The best responses engage confidently with the unseen poem, make comparison continuous rather than saving it for a final paragraph, and comment on the effect of a technique rather than simply naming it. They also answer the exact wording of the task without repeating that wording so often that it becomes intrusive.

The most common error is assuming that the two poets must agree. They frequently do not, and the differences between them are where the highest marks are earned. Read the unseen poem for how it departs from your anthology poem, not only for how it echoes it.

Writing about only one of the two poems in part (a). However good the analysis, a one-poem answer cannot rise past the lower bands.

Choosing a part (b) poem from a different cluster, or a poem that is no longer in the current anthology.

Re-using the part (a) anthology poem in part (b). It must be a different poem.

Comparing in part (b). Comparison is not required there, and it eats the time you need for close analysis of one poem.

How This Unit Works

The next three lessons build the analytical toolkit: language and imagery, then form and structure, then theme and personal response. Lesson five puts them together into the central skill of this paper: linking an unfamiliar poem to the cluster you know. The final lesson turns all of it into a timed routine.

242f3166-ab45-4c6d-af73-6cc404d73088.title: Analysing Language & Imagery
242f3166-ab45-4c6d-af73-6cc404d73088.content_html:
Why Language Analysis Carries This Section

In the comparison part of the poetry section, analysis of the poet’s methods is the dominant objective. That means the marks come from explaining what a word does, not from naming a device. Examiners call the weaker habit feature-spotting. A response that lists metaphor, alliteration and enjambment without explaining any of their effects sits low in the bands, however many terms it uses.

Key Fact

Every analytical point should make three moves: quote a few words, say what those particular words suggest, then say why that matters to the idea the poet is building. Two images analysed this way earn more than ten techniques that are only named.

Imagery: What Is Being Transferred?

When you meet a simile or a metaphor, do not stop at naming it. Ask what qualities move from one thing to the other. Byron opens ‘The Destruction of Sennacherib’ with “The Assyrian came down like the wolf on the fold”. The simile gives the army a predator’s hunger and speed, but the more telling word is “fold”, which turns the victims into penned sheep: animals that are owned, counted and unable to escape. The slaughter is made to feel routine as well as violent.

An extended metaphor deserves even more attention. If a single comparison runs through a poem, it is almost certainly carrying the poem’s central idea, and it should anchor your response rather than appear as one point among many.

Personification gives human life to something that has none. In Wordsworth’s boat-stealing episode, “a huge peak, black and huge” seems to rise and stride after the boy. The mountain has not moved; the boy’s guilt makes it seem to. The personification turns the landscape into an image of the boy’s conscience.

Pathetic fallacy is the narrower case where weather or season mirrors feeling. Students spot it easily but often stop there. The mark comes from precision. Do not write “the rain shows sadness”; say what kind of sadness the particular weather implies.

Symbol is an object that carries meaning beyond itself. Watch for anything a poet returns to. A repeated object in a short poem is usually deliberate.

Connotation: Testing a Poet’s Word Choice

The most useful habit in unseen analysis is testing a word’s connotations against its alternatives. Emily Dickinson begins “There’s a certain Slant of light”. She could have written a beam, a shaft, a ray. “Slant” suggests something oblique and slightly wrong, and that crookedness prepares the reader for the pain the poem goes on to describe.

Ask yourself what would be lost if the poet had used the ordinary word instead. Your answer to that question is the point to write down.

Verbs repay this test more than any other word class. They carry the energy of a line, and poets choose them precisely. Whether a speaker walks, drifts, trudges or strides tells you almost everything about their state of mind, and the shift from an active verb to a passive construction often marks the moment a speaker loses control of their own story.

Semantic Fields

A semantic field is a cluster of words drawn from one area of life. Mary Lamb’s ‘Envy’ judges the envious mind with words of failed sight and sensation — the rose tree that cannot see “its own red rose” is called “blind and senseless”. Naming a semantic field is a strong move in an unseen poem because it lets you make one point about the whole text rather than a scattering of small ones.

Sibilance, the repetition of soft s sounds, can hush a line or make it hiss, depending on the context.

Plosives — b, d, p, t, k, g — stop the air abruptly and suit anger, force or shock.

Vowel length changes pace. Keats opens with “Bright star, would I were stedfast as thou art”, and the long open vowels hold the line steady, imitating the fixed star the speaker envies. Short vowels would have hurried it and destroyed the effect.

Key Fact

“The poet uses sibilance” earns nothing. “The soft s sounds slow the line to a whisper, so the threat seems to creep rather than strike” earns the mark. The difference is always the same: name the effect on the reader, and tie it to the poem’s idea.

Language Inside a Comparison

In the comparison part, resist analysing one poem’s language completely before turning to the other. Put the two images beside each other in the same paragraph. If one poet reaches for a predator and the other for a machine, that contrast is itself a point about attitude — and it earns credit under both objectives at once.

50585cf6-b6db-4202-b235-517ac8b8ff76.title: Linking the Unseen Poem to Your Anthology Cluster
50585cf6-b6db-4202-b235-517ac8b8ff76.content_html:
How the Comparison Task Works

This is the skill the poetry section is built around. You are given a named poem from your anthology cluster and an unfamiliar poem chosen to link to it, both printed on the paper, and a single instruction: compare how they present the theme the task names. All twenty marks depend on how well you keep the two poems together.

Key Fact

A response that writes about only one of the two poems — the anthology poem or the unseen one — cannot rise beyond the lower mark bands, no matter how skilled the analysis. Both poems must be present throughout. Analysis of method is the dominant objective in this part, so the comparison must be about how each poet writes, not only about what each poem says.

Step One: Read the Unseen Poem Through the Theme

Read the task first, then the unseen poem with that theme in mind. You are not trying to understand everything the poem does; you are trying to find what it says about the one idea you have been asked about. Annotate only against that idea. Time spent on anything else is time you will need later.

Step Two: Decide Whether They Agree

This is the decision that shapes the whole answer, and it is where responses most often go wrong. Students assume that because two poems are linked by theme, the poets must think alike. They frequently do not. A thematic link guarantees a common subject, not a common attitude.

Same idea, different feeling. Both poems may mourn a lost love, but one is bitter and one is calm. Use the shared idea to set up the paragraph, then make the difference in feeling your main point.

Same feeling, different method. Both poems build unease — one through broken lines and caesura, the other through a stanza that lengthens without reaching a full stop. When two poets reach the same effect by opposite means, that contrast makes excellent comparative writing.

Direct disagreement. Sometimes the unseen poem contradicts your anthology poem outright. Say so plainly, and build the whole response around that disagreement. This is the strongest structure available to you.

Step Three: Build a Grid in Five Minutes

Draw four rows down the margin of your answer booklet — idea and attitude, tone, language, structure — and two columns, one per poem. Fill it with short quotations only. Those four rows are the three bullet prompts the task gives you, split so that method has two rows instead of one. Each completed row is a paragraph, already comparative before you write a sentence.

Key Fact

Use the grid as your plan. Four rows — idea and attitude, tone, language, structure — and two columns, one for the anthology poem and one for the unseen poem. Five minutes spent filling it saves you from the block structure that costs marks, because every row already contains both poems.

Step Four: Write Alternately, Not in Blocks

The weakest structure discusses poem one for three paragraphs, then poem two for three paragraphs, then compares briefly at the end. The strongest is interwoven comparison: one comparative idea per paragraph, both poems inside it, evidence from each.

Comparative connectives carry that structure — whereas, by contrast, similarly, where one poet does this, the other does that. Use them honestly. A connective that promises similarity in front of a point that is really a contrast is worse than no connective at all.

A Worked Comparison

Suppose the anthology poem is Emily Brontë’s ‘Love and Friendship’ and the unseen poem is Thomas Hardy’s ‘Neutral Tones’, with the task asking how the poems present love that has failed.

Both poets judge love through the natural world, but they reach opposite verdicts. Brontë sets “Love is like the wild rose-briar” against “Friendship like the holly-tree”, using the seasonal cycle as a test that love fails and friendship survives: the holly will “bloom most constantly”. Hardy allows no such consolation. His speaker recalls how “We stood by a pond that winter day”, and the pond offers neither renewal nor endurance — only stillness.

The comparison then moves to method. Brontë’s regular quatrains and simple similes make her argument feel settled, almost proverbial, as though the lesson has already been learned. Hardy’s image of a sun that is “white, as though chidden of God” drains the scene of warmth and colour, so that the failure of love is presented not as a lesson but as a stain the speaker cannot wash out.

Notice what the paragraph does not do. It never summarises either poem, it quotes no more than a handful of words at a time, and it never abandons one poem to deal with the other separately. Every sentence keeps both texts in view.

Three Things Not to Do

Do not summarise the poems before comparing them; the examiner has both texts in front of them. Do not save comparison for the conclusion. And do not invent context for the unseen poem — you cannot know who wrote it or when, and background earns no marks in this section anyway.

6ac8cb2a-b621-4d9a-9658-026e311f6fcd.title: Analysing Form & Structure
6ac8cb2a-b621-4d9a-9658-026e311f6fcd.content_html:
Why Form and Structure Matter

The dominant objective in the comparison part names three things: language, form and structure. Most students write well about the first and almost nothing about the other two. That is the easiest place in the whole paper to pick up marks, because form and structure are visible before you have understood a single line.

Form is the kind of poem it is. Structure is the order in which it releases its ideas. Form is the container; structure is the journey inside it.

Key Fact

You can see the number of stanzas, whether the lines are regular or ragged, and whether the poem narrows or widens towards the end — all before you read a word. Those observations are already analysis of form, and in an unseen poem they buy you a point while you are still working out the meaning.

Form: The Shape the Poet Chose

A sonnet promises fourteen lines and an argument that turns. Keats uses one for “Bright star, would I were stedfast as thou art”, and the tight, closed form suits a speaker longing for permanence. A ballad, with its regular beat and repeated refrain, suits storytelling and public grief. Free verse abandons a fixed pattern altogether, which can feel like natural speech — or like control breaking down.

Key Fact

Never write “this is a sonnet” and stop. Naming a form earns nothing. The mark comes from the consequence: what does the form let this poet do, or stop them doing, that another shape would not?

Where does it begin and end emotionally? Track the feeling from the first line to the last. A poem that opens in anger and closes in exhaustion has a structure worth describing.

Where is the turn? Look for a stanza break, a conjunction, or a shift of tense or pronoun.

What repeats? Repetition of a word, a line or a grammatical pattern is structural, and it usually signals obsession, insistence or ritual.

How do the final lines land? Look for resolution, refusal, or a deliberate failure to resolve. Endings are the most quotable structural evidence you have.

The Turn

A volta is the hinge of a poem. Emily Brontë’s ‘Love and Friendship’ sets “Love is like the wild rose-briar” against “Friendship like the holly-tree”, then turns from the showy rose to the plant that will “bloom most constantly”. The turn carries the argument, so finding it usually tells you what the poem is trying to say.

Line-Level Structure

Enjambment spills a sentence past the line break and hurries the reader onward; it can suggest breathlessness, overflow or a thought the speaker cannot contain. A caesura does the opposite, stopping a line in its middle. An end-stopped line closes cleanly and can feel controlled, final or stubborn.

These are useful because they need no knowledge of the poet. You can hear them on a first reading of an unfamiliar poem.

Rhyme works the same way. A tight, regular rhyme scheme can make a poem sound settled and inevitable — useful when a poet wants an argument to feel proved. Half-rhyme, where the sounds almost but do not quite match, unsettles the ear and often signals something the speaker cannot resolve. If a regular scheme suddenly breaks, that break is a structural event and deserves a sentence of its own.

Two poems on one theme are often built to do opposite things, and that contrast is one of the strongest comparative points available to you. One poem may tighten towards a controlled final couplet while the other loosens into fragments.

Compare the endings directly. Where a poem chooses to stop tells you what its poet believes about the subject: whether the problem can be resolved, survived, or only stated.

If both poems share a feature — both use enjambment, say — do not stop at the similarity. Ask what each poet uses it for. Identical methods put to different purposes make an excellent paragraph.

Terminology You Can Always Use Safely

Stanza, quatrain, couplet, refrain, rhyme scheme, half-rhyme, enjambment, caesura, volta, free verse, first person, present tense. Every one of these can be applied to a poem you have never seen, and every one can be tied to an effect. Accurate terminology is credited — but only when it is attached to an explanation.

d88323aa-2611-4bd2-80be-299975c28abd.title: Exam Technique & Timed Practice
d88323aa-2611-4bd2-80be-299975c28abd.content_html:
The Paper in Numbers

Everything in this lesson comes from three figures. The poetry and Shakespeare paper is two hours long, worth 80 marks, and taken closed text — no anthology, no play, nothing on the desk. Eighty marks in a hundred and twenty minutes gives you exactly one and a half minutes per mark, and every timing below is that figure applied.

Key Fact

The paper is two hours long and worth eighty marks. Forty marks go to the poetry section and forty to the Shakespeare section, so each deserves an even hour. Inside the poetry hour, part (a) and part (b) are worth twenty marks each — so they deserve thirty minutes each, planning included.

The Poetry Hour, Minute by Minute

0–5 min

Read the task, then both poems

Task first so you know the theme. Then read the anthology poem and the unseen poem, annotating only against that theme.

5–8 min

Fill the comparison grid

Idea and attitude, tone, language, structure — two columns, short quotations only.

8–30 min

Write part (a)

A comparative thesis, then three or four interwoven paragraphs. Both poems in every paragraph.

30–34 min

Choose and plan part (b)

Pick a different poem from your cluster and write your thesis sentence before you start.

34–58 min

Write part (b)

Detailed exploration of that single poem. No comparison.

58–60 min

Check and move on

Check quotations, then leave for the Shakespeare section on the hour whatever state the answer is in.

Key Fact

Part (b) is the most commonly rushed answer on this paper. Examiners report that responses are often brief, as if timing had been forgotten under pressure. It carries exactly the same twenty marks as the comparison. A thin part (b) costs as much as a thin part (a), and it is the easier of the two to fix.

Rubric Mistakes That Cost Whole Answers

A rubric infringement is a failure to read the instructions rather than a failure of skill, and it caps an answer that might otherwise have scored well. These four are the ones examiners see every year.

Answering on only one poem in part (a). The comparison must cover the anthology poem and the unseen poem together.

Choosing a part (b) poem from a different cluster, or one that has been removed from the current anthology. Check your cluster list before the exam, not during it.

Re-using the part (a) anthology poem in part (b). The task asks for one other poem, so the part (a) poem cannot be used again.

Comparing in part (b). No comparison is required there, and it steals the time you need for close analysis of one text.

What a Strong Answer Looks Like on the Page

Length does not earn marks. Examiners report very long scripts — some running to fifteen sides or more — whose quality suffered from their length, with the same point restated through one quotation after another. Three or four developed, interwoven paragraphs beat eight thin ones.

Keep quotations embedded and short. Four well-placed words prove more than a copied-out stanza, and they leave room for the analysis that actually earns the mark.

Two Practical Points About the Booklet

Spelling, punctuation and grammar are not assessed in the poetry section, so do not spend your final minutes proofreading. Legibility is a different matter: examiners regularly report scripts they struggle to decipher even when magnified. A mark cannot be given for a word that cannot be read.

Label your answers clearly as part (a) and part (b), and start part (b) on a fresh page. It costs nothing and it removes any doubt about which poem belongs to which task.

Week one. Untimed. Take an unfamiliar short poem, spend fifteen minutes filling a comparison grid against a cluster poem, and write nothing else. Grid practice is the highest-value drill there is.

Week two. Thirty minutes for part (a) alone, twice. Mark yourself on one question only: does every paragraph contain both poems?

Week three. Thirty minutes for part (b) alone, twice, on different cluster poems. Check your quotations against the text afterwards and count the misquotations.

Week four. The full poetry hour, both parts, in one sitting, twice. This is the only drill that tests whether you can stop part (a) on time.

The Final Check

Before you turn the page: does part (a) discuss both poems in every paragraph? Does part (b) cover a different poem from your own cluster, without comparison? Have you explained the effect of every method you named? If all three answers are yes, the answer is doing what the mark scheme asks.
